T-6A Flight Manual Change 3
This document summarizes:
1) It is the flight manual for the USAF/USN T-6A aircraft made by Hawker Beechcraft Corporation, superseding previous interim supplements and safety supplements. 
2) It provides instructions and warnings for use, distribution, and destruction of the manual in accordance with US defense regulations.
3) The manual contains over 470 pages of instructions and procedures for operating the T-6A aircraft.

INTRODUCTION                                                   DEFINITIONS
This section contains procedures to be followed in the event   Land As Soon As Possible
of an emergency. These procedures will ensure maximum
safety for the crew and/or aircraft until a safe landing or    An emergency shall be declared and a landing accomplished
other appropriate action is accomplished. Although the pro-    at the nearest suitable landing area considering the severity
cedures contained herein are considered the best available,    of the emergency, weather conditions, field facilities, ambi-
pilots must exercise sound judgment when confronted with       ent lighting, and command guidance.
an emergency.
                                                               Land As Soon As Practical
When an airborne emergency occurs, three basic rules
apply. These rules should be thoroughly understood by all      Emergency conditions are less urgent and, although the mis-
pilots:                                                        sion is to be terminated, the degree of the emergency is such
                                                               that an immediate landing may not be necessary.
  ● Maintain aircraft control.
  ● Analyze the situation and take proper action.              Suitable Landing Area
  ● Land as soon as conditions permit.                         A suitable landing area is a hard surface runway, taxiway, or
                                                               under/overrun. Landing on an unprepared surface or ditch-
CRITICAL ACTION (US AIR FORCE)                                 ing is not recommended.
Procedures appearing in CAPITAL BOLD FACE LET-
TERS are considered CRITICAL action. CRITICAL                  CREW COORDINATION
actions are items that must be performed immediately if the    Essential steps or items which are to be checked in both
emergency is not to be aggravated, and injury or damage are    cockpits, if occupied, are indicated by (BOTH) following
to be avoided. These CRITICAL steps will be committed to       the step.
memory.

CRITICAL ACTION (US NAVY)
                                                               The term “reset” is used to describe the action of resetting a
Items indicated with an asterisk (*) are memory items that     circuit breaker that is already open. The pilot should assess
may result in serious injury or death and/or damage to         the severity of the emergency, equipment lost, and the bene-
equipment if not carefully and expeditiously executed.         fits gained prior to resetting or opening any circuit breaker.

checklist. Time permitting, review/complete the procedures     ered without the affected equipment, the circuit breaker
utilizing the pocket checklist to ensure completeness.         should not be reset.
NONCRITICAL ACTION
Those actions which contribute to an orderly sequence of
events, improve the chances for emergency action to be suc-
cessful, and serve as “clean-up” items.

NOTES
1. N1 values presented for PMU ON. With PMU OFF, N1 may vary from these values.
2. With PMU OFF, permissible maximum NP is 100±2%.
3. Permissible at all powers for completion of flight in emergency.
4. Avoid stabilized ground operation from 62 to 80% NP.
5. Operation in this range permitted only during aerobatics or spins, and 15 to 40 psi for 5 seconds with PCL at IDLE.
6. Normal oil pressure during steady state conditions is 90 to 120 psi. Operation at oil pressure less than 90 psi at flight idle or
   above is indicative of oil system malfunction.
7. Acceptable for ground operation at and below 20% torque.
8. Torque at 131% is a materials limit above which damage to the engine may occur. Torque above 102% is indicative of a
system malfunction.

RCR is a measure of the braking friction coefficient. RCR is
given as a whole number. Values vary from 26 (the maxi-
mum braking friction coefficient), to 2 (the minimum brak-                                           Runway Length
ing friction coefficient). This value is used to define the                                          Runway length is the paved surface length excluding any
braking characteristics for various runway surface condi-                                            overrun.
tions. The reported RCR is therefore a factor in determining
any performance data which involves braking. Some air-                                               Runway Available
fields report runway braking characteristics in accordance
with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) stan-                                          Runway available is the runway length minus the aircraft
                                                                                                     lineup distance.

RUNWAY CONDITION READING (RCR)                                                                                       Dry                       Good                          23
RCR is a measure of the braking friction coefficient. RCR is                                                        Wet                      Medium                          12
given as a whole number. Values vary from 26 (the maxi-
mum braking friction coefficient), to 2 (the minimum brak-                                                           Icy                        Poor                         05
ing friction coefficient). This value is used to define the
braking characteristics for various runway surface condi-                                            AIR DISTANCE
tions. The reported RCR is therefore a factor in determining
any performance data which involves braking. Some air-                                               Air distance is the ground distance covered from the 50-foot
fields report runway braking characteristics in accordance                                           obstacle height to touchdown.

INTRODUCTION                                                                                         MISSION PLANNING SUMMARY
Mission planning is a critical part of every flight. This pro-                                       Figure A9-1 presents a summary of the mission planning
cedure begins with assignment of the aircraft and includes,                                          example.
but is not limited to, the determination of fuel required, cal-
culation of the weight and balance profile for the entire                                            TAKEOFF AND LANDING DATA (TOLD) CARD
flight, ensuring compliance with weight and balance limita-                                          Figure A9-2 presents a takeoff and landing data (TOLD)
tions, takeoff and landing runway requirements, flight per-                                          card.
formance, flight planning, and crew briefings. Refer to the
appropriate Section or Appendix Part for limitations and                                             WEIGHT AND CG VERIFICATION
performance data.

                                                                                                     Weight, and Takeoff CG of the aircraft.

Common questions
Powered by AI
What factors influence the specific range calculation of an aircraft at sea level under standard temperature?
Specific range at sea level under standard temperature is influenced by aircraft weight and airspeed. For example, with an aircraft weight of 6000 pounds and airspeed of 151 KIAS, the specific range can be determined by reflecting up to weight on a grid and then left to read the range, which demonstrates the importance of weight and speed in range calculations .
In what scenario would a pilot use the "OBS mode" on the GPS, and how is it activated?
The OBS mode is used to define the course to the active waypoint and is crucial for flying non-precision approaches using GPS. It can be activated by toggling the OBS mode button, which switches the system between Enroute/Leg and OBS modes .
What are the steps involved in executing a forced landing when the engine is unavailable?
In a forced landing with no engine, maintain the ELP profile, avoid extending landing gear on unprepared surfaces, and manage airspeed and flaps as required. Important steps include retracting gear if landing unprepared, using flaps only if gear is extended, and planning increased landing distance for zero power .
Describe how the nearest airports and VORs are displayed on the aircraft's GPS system.
The GPS system computes the nine nearest airports, VORs, and NDBs. By rotating the right outer knob to select APT, VOR, or NDB, and pulling the right inner knob to the out position, the list of waypoints can be navigated. The nearest waypoints are labeled NR 1 to NR 9, with the nearest positioned at the top. Detailed information like runway length and surface is displayed for airports .
How does the process of creating a new user waypoint on the GPS system work?
To create a user waypoint, select the SUP page using the right outer knob, activate the cursor with the right CRSR button, and use the outer and inner knobs to set the waypoint identifier. If the identifier is unused, one can create a waypoint at present position or other specified locations by pressing the SAVE button and accepting the new waypoint if a unique identifier is entered .
What procedure should be followed if both OBOGS regulators are not deactivated during aircraft shutdown?
If both OBOGS regulators are not deactivated, it will drain the aircraft battery even if all other electrical switches are off. This stresses the importance of ensuring that the OBOGS supply lever is turned off to prevent unnecessary battery discharge .
Why is it important for the canopy to be closed prior to engine start under manual mode?
Closing the canopy before starting the engine in manual mode is crucial to prevent injury or damage due to exhaust and prop wash. It ensures the pilot's safety and prevents any operational issues with the canopy .
How does the GPS system on an aircraft manage power and memory storage during operation?
Each GPS unit includes a battery for non-volatile memory, allowing storage of flight plans and other user data even during power interruptions. The system requires the front unit to be on and functioning for navigation, and it is powered through a circuit breaker on the battery bus circuit breaker panel in the front cockpit and the generator bus circuit breaker panel in the rear cockpit .
How should a blown tire be handled post-landing according to the guidelines, and why is this critical?
Upon detecting a blown tire during landing, maintain flap settings, and aim to land on the side of the runway with the intact tire to maintain control. This is critical to prevent directional instability and potential runway departure, which could result in further aircraft damage or injury .
What effect does a loss of the PMU have on aircraft engine control, and how should it be managed?
A PMU failure results in the loss of automatic control of torque, ITT, and N1, necessitating manual control to manage engine parameters. Propeller governing, including overspeed protection, is still provided by a mechanical governor. The pilot should switch the PMU OFF and continue flying with minimal practical power to mitigate power shifts .
